name: Micro-expressions

card.summary: Fleeting involuntary facial expressions lasting under half a second, studied for reading emotion and used by people who want to improve their expressiveness and read faces.
card.note: Lie-detection claims about micro-expressions are disputed by researchers.

quick.overview:
A micro-expression is a very brief facial expression, usually under half a second, that flashes across the face when someone has an emotion they are trying to hide or suppress. The idea goes back to Haggard and Isaacs in 1966 and was developed by Paul Ekman and Wallace Friesen.

In looksmaxxing and social-skills circles it relates to how the face communicates: people interested in charisma and face reading study expressions to come across as warmer and to read others. Training tools exist, and researchers also build computer-vision systems to detect micro-expressions.
quick.how: People use video training tools such as the micro and subtle facial expression training tools, which present clips and give feedback, and some practise expression in a mirror or on camera.
quick.risks: There are no physical risks. Researchers dispute how well micro-expressions reveal deception, and critics warn against using them to judge suspects or strangers.

lead: A micro-expression is a brief facial expression, typically lasting under half a second, produced when voluntary and involuntary emotional responses conflict so that a true feeling shows briefly before a false one replaces it [1]. Haggard and Isaacs first described 'micro-momentary' expressions in 1966 while scanning psychotherapy films, and Paul Ekman and Wallace Friesen later found agreement on emotion labels across cultures, including among the Fore people of Papua New Guinea [1][7].

Expression is one part of how a face is perceived, alongside structure, skin and grooming. Interest in micro-expressions in looksmaxxing and social-skills circles is mainly about emotional signalling: learning how feelings show on the face, how others read them, and how to present a warmer, more engaged expression. Training tools called MFETT and SFETT are used to improve recognition, often with people who find social situations difficult [1][7].

Researchers have questioned the lie-detection claims. A 2008 study that coded 700 high-stakes expressions found only 2% were micro-expressions, appearing equally in truth-tellers and liars [1]. A separate field of computer vision builds databases and algorithms to detect micro-expressions automatically [2][3][9].

chain: Learn how emotion shows on the face
Expressions become more deliberate and natural
angle.text: People study micro-expressions to understand how emotion shows on the face and to improve their own expression and social reading. It concerns expression, not bone structure.

infobox: Disgust, anger, fear, sadness, happiness, contempt, surprise [1]

paras: Wikipedia distinguishes simulated, neutralized and masked micro-expressions: a flash of expression over a neutral face, a suppressed genuine emotion, and a genuine emotion covered by a fake one [1]. Ekman's list of universal emotions is disgust, anger, fear, sadness, happiness, contempt and surprise, and he later expanded the set to include states such as amusement, embarrassment and pride [1]. Display rules, shaped by culture and family, govern which expressions people show, often automatically [1].

Emotions typically last from minutes to an hour, while moods last a day or longer; micro-expressions are the briefest layer, with high-speed cameras able to capture them for slow-motion replay [1]. Neuroscience work has examined the brain basis of spontaneous expressions and micro-expressions, including an EEG study of functional brain networks [11][13].

Haggard and Isaacs described micro-momentary expressions in 1966 while scanning psychotherapy films, and in the 1960s William Condon analysed a 4.5-second film segment frame by frame over roughly a year and a half [1]. Paul Ekman, born in 1934, earned his PhD at Adelphi University in 1958, joined the University of California, San Francisco in 1972 and retired in 2004; with Wallace Friesen he developed the Facial Action Coding System by 1978, which describes facial movement as anatomically defined action units [7]. Ekman died in November 2025 [7].

In studies with Friesen, people across Western and Eastern cultures and the preliterate Fore of Papua New Guinea matched emotion labels to expressions, with the strongest agreement for anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness and surprise and less clear support for contempt [1][7]. Ekman also ran the Wizards Project with Maureen O'Sullivan on people who read deception unusually well, reporting about 50 such 'naturals' among 20,000 tested [7]. Matsumoto's study of sighted and blind judo athletes at the 2004 Olympic and Paralympic Games found similar winning and losing expressions, which the Wikipedia article reads as evidence that they are not learned visually [1].

sections.h: Training tools and use for self-presentation
paras: MFETT and SFETT are software tools that teach emotion recognition through instructional videos, practice faces and immediate feedback, and they are often used with people who find social situations difficult, such as those with autism [1][7]. Daniel Goleman linked the ability to read facial emotion to emotional intelligence, and Wikipedia describes mirror neurons and emotional contagion as explanations for how one person's expression affects an observer [1].

In appearance and charisma communities, people use such ideas in general terms: studying how a smile engages the eyes, how a neutral or tense resting face is read by others, and rehearsing expressions in a mirror or on video. Pilot trials of recognition training exist for medical students and for people with schizophrenia [4][5].

Wikipedia reports lie-detection accuracy averaging about 54% for ordinary people and 64% for Secret Service agents, with an Ekman-linked cohort of motivated participants reaching 68-73% [1]. In 2008 Porter and ten Brinke coded 700 high-stakes emotional expressions and found only 2% were micro-expressions, appearing equally often in truth-tellers and liars [1]. Pentland and colleagues reported liars showing less contempt and more intense smiles than truthful people [1]. Wikipedia states that micro-expressions reveal emotional arousal rather than the concealed content, so they do not determine whether someone is lying [1]. John Gottman's couples research found Ekman's facial coding was not statistically significant, while skin conductance and oral-history narratives were [1].

Critics including Maria Hartwig argue that reliance on such cues has contributed to wrongful imprisonment after aggressive interrogations, and a 2016 Scientific Reports study found people fail to tell real from masked expressions over 40% of the time [1]. Critics of Ekman's methodology argue that some of his studies were circular because subjects matched photos to the same emotion labels he used, and that parts of his later work were not peer reviewed [7].

Computer scientists have built datasets such as CASME II and recognition systems for automatic micro-expression analysis, with surveys covering databases, features, algorithms and challenges [2][3][9][10].

sections.h: Security screening and the SPOT program
paras: The US Transportation Security Administration trained behaviour-detection officers from 2006 and deployed the Screening of Passengers by Observation Techniques (SPOT) program at airports in 2007; it was renamed Behavior Detection and Analysis in 2016 [8]. Wikipedia says the program was originally based on Ekman's Facial Action Coding System, that its 94 criteria related to stress, fear or deception, and that these were kept secret until The Intercept published them in March 2015 [8]. A 2015 Hacker News thread discussed the program under the title 'Be careful with your face at airports' [6].

The program cost about $900 million in its first six years, with around 2,800 employees working on it as of 2015 [8]. In 2010 the Government Accountability Office criticised the TSA for deploying it without scientific validation, and a 2013 GAO report and a DHS Inspector General report found little evidence of effectiveness; funding was later reduced [8]. Judee Burgoon cites testimony that 0.6% of 61,000 passenger referrals in 2011 and 2012 led to arrests [1]. Critics, including the ACLU, argued the program led to profiling; Philip Rubin testified to Congress in 2011 that it lacked scientific evaluation [8].

The 2009 TV series Lie to Me was based on Ekman's work, and its lead character Dr. Lightman was modelled on him, with Ekman serving as scientific adviser [1][7]. Wikipedia also lists appearances in The Mentalist, in novels by Robert Ludlum and Alastair Reynolds, and in the 2015 film Ex Machina [1]. Ekman was named to the Time 100 list in 2009 and advised Pixar on the 2015 film Inside Out [7].

Studies include a pilot of micro-expression recognition training in medical students [4], a pilot of emotion-recognition remediation in schizophrenia using a micro-expression training tool [5], and technical surveys of recognition datasets and algorithms [2][3]. Other work has examined whether facial expressions captured on video can help detect Parkinson's disease [12].

timeline.event: Haggard and Isaacs identify micro-momentary expressions [1].
Ekman and Friesen report cross-cultural agreement on emotion labels [1].
Ekman and Friesen complete the Facial Action Coding System [7].
TSA begins training behaviour-detection officers after the British liquid bomb plot; the SPOT program reaches US airports in 2007 [8].
Porter and ten Brinke coding study of 700 expressions [1].
Lie to Me premieres; Ekman is named to the Time 100 [1][7].
GAO criticises SPOT for deployment without scientific validation [8].
GAO and DHS Inspector General reports find little evidence the program works [8].
CASME II spontaneous micro-expression database published [10].
SPOT renamed Behavior Detection and Analysis [8].
Paul Ekman dies in San Francisco [7].

lore.intro: In looksmaxxing and social-skills discussion, micro-expressions come up as part of charisma and face reading, and are often linked with Hollywood portrayals of lie detection [1][7].

claims.claim: Micro-expressions reveal when someone is lying
claims.believers: Proponents, drawing on Ekman's work and the TV series it inspired, say brief flashes of concealed emotion leak through [1][7].
claims.experts: A 2008 coding study found only 2% of expressions were micro-expressions, equally in truth-tellers and liars, and Wikipedia states they reveal arousal rather than the concealed content [1].

claims.claim: Training improves your ability to read emotions
claims.believers: Users of MFETT and SFETT report better recognition of subtle expressions, and the tools are used with people who find social situations difficult [1][7].
claims.experts: Pilot studies of recognition training exist in medical students and in people with schizophrenia [4][5].

claims.claim: Emotional expressions are universal across cultures
claims.believers: Ekman and Friesen's studies, including among the Fore people, found agreement on emotion labels for basic emotions [1][7].
claims.experts: Critics say some of the research design was circular, and contempt's universality had less clear support [1][7].

claims.claim: Airport behaviour screening can spot dangerous people from facial cues
claims.believers: The TSA's SPOT program was originally based on Ekman's work [8][6].
claims.experts: The GAO and DHS Inspector General found little evidence of effectiveness, and critics raised profiling concerns [8].

claims.claim: People can learn to read others' faces better to come across as more charismatic
claims.believers: Social-skills communities link reading and showing emotion to emotional intelligence, citing Goleman [1].
claims.experts: No published studies have tested micro-expression practice as a way to improve perceived attractiveness or charisma.
